children.text: Republican Rudolph Giuliani defeated incumbent David Dinkins in New York City's mayoral race by the narrowest of margins, with 60 percent of Latino/a voters backing the losing candidate. Reports emerged of intimidating flyers in the Dominican neighborhood of Washington Heights warning voters that poll watchers would be checking passports, prompting a federal investigation. In Miami, Miriam Alonso and Steve Clark headed to a November 9th runoff after election day voting broke sharply along ethnic lines. California voters rejected the school voucher initiative Proposition 174 by a two-to-one margin. NAFTA proponents in Congress still needed 48 additional votes ahead of the mid-November House vote, with immigration restrictionists using the debate to argue the treaty did too little to curb undocumented entry. Teachers in Puerto Rico went on strike over a school voucher program they said threatened public education, and residents of the island of Vieques pressed President Clinton to add the Navy's bases there to a base closure list after bombs were reportedly dropped near a residential area.
Election Analysis: New York and Miami

Political analyst Gerson Borrero and El Nuevo Herald reporter Ivan Roman joined Maria Hinojosa to break down the two mayoral races. Borrero noted that New York Latino/as turned out at about 20 percent of the electorate and voted along Democratic lines but did not constitute a decisive swing vote. Roman described a generational divide among Miami Cuban voters, with younger Cuban Americans rejecting the ethnic ownership appeals that older voters responded to, and Puerto Rican and Nicaraguan voters in Miami pushing back against messaging that framed the mayor's seat as exclusively Cuban American. Both analysts were skeptical of the interpretation that the results represented a broad rebuke of the Clinton administration.
Dia de los Muertos and the AIDS Crisis

Community groups in Austin and San Antonio were using Day of the Dead traditions to address the AIDS epidemic in Latino/a communities, where the disease had become the leading killer of young Hispanic men and the third leading cause of death among Latinas ages 25 to 44. An East Austin altar exhibit organized by an AIDS outreach group featured non-traditional elements like condoms alongside flowers and photographs, aiming to break the silence and stigma surrounding AIDS deaths in families. A San Antonio performance artist created a piece drawing on the death of a close friend from AIDS, connecting personal loss to broader patterns of homophobia and machismo in Chicane families. A theater group of young people called the Cultural Warriors at an Austin alternative high school staged skits drawn from their own experiences with loss, using the Day of the Dead framework to speak openly about death from drugs, AIDS, and violence.

Pianist Eddie Palmieri, who had been pushing the creative limits of Latin music for over three decades, sat for a profile tracing his career from early dance hall battles at the Palladium to the dissolution of his celebrated ensemble La Perfecta to a new recording contract with Elektra Asylum. Palmieri described moving toward a deeper focus on Afro-Caribbean jazz composition while rooting his work firmly in Latin rhythms, which he credited with creative vitality that extends back tens of thousands of years.
John Guardo: Speaking for the Street

Colombian-born commentator John Guardo, 21, reflected on his years as a member of a New York City crew and the drug culture that surrounded it. He described watching dealers rise and fall and witnessing friends deteriorate, and recalled the night a 21-year-old friend overdosed on cocaine and died of a heart attack hours after Guardo had left the gathering where the drugs were present.
